newsitem.title: USA: Senate Superfund proposal would cost $2 bln a year.
newsitem.headline: Senate Superfund proposal would cost $2 bln a year.

text.p: A new proposal to speed up cleanups of the worst U.S. toxic waste dumps could cost the government $2 billion a year, Senate aides said Wednesday.

Staffers said costs had not officially been calculated yet, but had been estimated at $1.9 billion to $2.1 billion, or about 50 percent more than Congress has approved for Superfund spending over the last few years.

The bill, introduced Tuesday by Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Chair John Chafee and Sen. Bob Smith, seeks to speed cleanup of Superfund sites by reducing legal challenges over cleanup cost liability and cleanup standards.
It would stem legal challenges by exempting from liability at least two-thirds of the parties who are currently required to pay cleanup costs, an aide to Smith said.

The legislation would also eliminate some lawsuits by setting up a system to allocate costs based on how much waste a party dumped, instead of allocating costs based on who could pay the money, he said.
"The real concepts are fairness and efficiency," an aide to Chafee said at a briefing on the bill.
Chafee told reporters he intended to push the bill this year. Smith said he hoped it would pass before October.

Democrats and environmental groups complained they had not been consulted before the bill was introduced. But other groups, including the chemical industry and insurance groups said they had not been consulted either.
"If we are to make reforms to Superfund this year, it is critical that we work in a bipartisan manner," said Sen. Frank Lautenberg, the top Democrat on the Senate Superfund panel.
"If we are to amend the Superfund bill this year, we must not add greater burdens on taxpayers in order to remove burdens from the shoulders of responsible polluters," he said in a statement.
The Chemical Manufacturers Association (CMA) called the bill a good starting point for all parties, including states, municipalities and small businesses.
"It's evident that these folks are trying to reach out and offer up a mainstream bill," CMA spokesman Owen Kean said.

Kean said that with a combination of cleanup cost recovery from companies, fines, penalties, trust fund interest, and oil, chemical and corporate environmental taxes, which expired in 1995 and need to be renewed, the system could come up with enough money to pay for the new Republican proposal.
"The system can produce that kind of money if it is fully tapped," he said. Congress has allowed the administration to tap only $1.3 billion a year over the last few years.
